props.title: My Best Friend's Wedding
props.initialSlug: A wedding, a best friend, and a war.

sections.content: My Best Friend's Wedding revolutionized the romantic comedy by subverting every expectation of the genre. Julia Roberts plays Julianne, who realizes she loves her best friend Michael only after he announces his engagement to someone else. Unlike typical rom-coms like Sleepless in Seattle (1993) or While You Were Sleeping (1995), this film dares to let its protagonist be the villain. Roberts trades her trademark sunny persona for complex desperation, scheming to break up the wedding through increasingly unethical means. The film's genius lies in making us root for someone doing terrible things, then forcing us to confront why we wanted her to succeed.

sections.content: The film sparked a wave of darker, more complex romantic comedies that challenged the formula. In Her Shoes (2005) explored sisterly rivalry alongside romance, while Sweet Home Alabama (2002) complicated its love triangle with genuine character growth. Director P.J. Hogan's decision to cast Cameron Diaz as Kimmy, the "rival," was crucial - instead of making her a villain, she's genuinely loveable, forcing both Julianne and the audience to recognize there's no easy happy ending.

The film's soundtrack deserves special mention for reinventing how music functions in romantic comedies. Rather than just background emotion, songs like "I Say A Little Prayer" become full musical numbers that reveal character. This influenced later films like Music and Lyrics (2007) and 500 Days of Summer (2009) to integrate music more meaningfully into their narratives. Rupert Everett's performance as George, the gay best friend character, also helped evolve that trope beyond stereotypical sidekick territory. SUBHEAD: Breaking Rom-Com Conventions

sections.content: The film's most radical choice was its ending - letting the "wrong" couple stay together while our protagonist learns to be happy for them. This paved the way for more realistic romantic comedies like 500 Days of Summer (2009) and La La Land (2016) that don't force happy endings. The wedding scene's final musical number, "I Say A Little Prayer," transforms from a moment of manipulation earlier in the film to one of genuine celebration, showing how Julianne has grown.
